newsitem.title: UK: UK grain shipments go on, despite EU export moves.
newsitem.headline: UK grain shipments go on, despite EU export moves.

text.p: Britain will be able to carry on sending wheat to non-EU countries for the rest of the (July-June) season, despite EU moves to end exports, grain traders said.
Even though the EU's cereals management committee is no longer awarding open market licences for wheat at its regular tender, there are still enough open EU export licences around, they said.
"I think there are enough around. We may be a bit short, but we should be able to export enough," one trader said.
The end-of-year outlook for the wheat market may not be as bad as a Home Grown Cereals analysis published on Monday suggests, traders said.

According to the HGCA's latest report on supply and demand the UK faces being stuck with a large stock of wheat to carryover into the new year, when the current marketing year ends at the end of June.
It reckons on some 600,000-700,000 tonnes being available for export in May and June, the final two months of the marketing year.
"The (EU) Commission appears to have completed its third country export campaign, so UK wheat exports are now restricted to intra-EU business," the HGCA said.
But the export outlook for May and June is much better than the HGCA assumes, one trader said.
Although, the EU Commission has, as the HGCA points out, ended its export campaign, there are still enough still-valid EU export licences around for the UK to go on exporting, he said.
"The licences are still in circulation. They can be used anytime," he said.

He reckoned UK wheat exports in May could come to between 250,000 and 275,000 tonnes, with June "quite reasonable," he said noting that UK wheat for June would be cheaper than the first French new crop.
Wheat imports for 1996-97 as a whole would be well under official estimates, further reducing the likely end-of-year surplus, while milling wheat usage was higher, he said.
"I'd say the market view of the potential surplus is 50,000 to 100,000 tonnes," another trader said. "For it to be more than a maximum 125,000 tonnes would be astonishing."

Traders said more wheat is to head for Tunisia from Britain within days. British supplies may well be used to supply wheat under a new Tunisian tender, for which the deadline is Wednesday morning, one said. It is for five lots of 25,000 tonnes of wheat each.
